name: Sigiriya
info: Sigiriya, or Sinhagiri, the Lion Rock, is a rock fortress and palace complex in the Matale District of Sri Lanka, developed under King Kashyapa from 477 CE on a granite column about 180 metres high.

facts.made: King Kashyapa I (reigned 477–495 CE) according to the Cūḷavaṃsa, with alternative accounts naming his father Dhatusena as the main builder or a Buddhist community as the makers
facts.form: A fortified city on and around a granite column about 180 metres high: an upper palace with rock-cut cisterns, a mid-level terrace with the Lion Gate and the mirror wall, lower palaces, moats, walls and three kinds of garden
facts.where: In the northern Matale District near the town of Dambulla, Central Province, Sri Lanka
facts.known: the Lion Gate; the frescoes of the western rock face; the mirror wall and its graffiti poems; the water, boulder and terraced gardens; hydraulic systems, some still working; the story of Kashyapa and Moggallana

t: According to the Cūḷavaṃsa, Kashyapa seized the throne in 477 CE, moved his capital from Anuradhapura to the rock of Sigiriya and built his palace on its summit.
After Kashyapa's defeat in 495 CE the capital returned to Anuradhapura and Sigiriya became a Buddhist monastery complex that lasted until the 13th or 14th century.
Its mirror wall carries more than 1,500 poems written by visitors, the only evidence of poetry found from the Anuradhapura period.
dyk: The mirror wall was once so reflective that the king could see himself as he walked alongside it, and one of the verses scribbled on it, deciphered by Senarath Paranavithana, reads: "I am Budal. Came with hundreds of people to see Sigiriya. Since all the others wrote poems, I did not!"
ev: The Aligala rock shelter east of Sigiriya shows the earliest evidence of human habitation, in the Mesolithic Period
Buddhist monastic settlements were established on the western and northern slopes of the hills around the rock
Kashyapa I seized the throne and moved the capital from Anuradhapura to Sigiriya
Moggallana defeated Kashyapa, who died, and returned the capital to Anuradhapura
The monastery complex that followed Kashyapa's city survived until the 13th or 14th century
Major Jonathan Forbes of the British Army came upon the brushwood-covered summit of the rock

The Cultural Triangle Project began archaeological work on the entire city

sections.origins:
Sigiriya lies in the northern Matale District near the town of Dambulla in the Central Province of Sri Lanka, where a massive column of granite about 180 metres high rises abruptly from the low-lying plains that extend from the central mountain range. It is an inselberg, a hardened granite outcrop derived from a solidified magma plug of a former volcano, and Pidurangala Rock, one kilometre to the north, has a similar origin. The area was probably inhabited since prehistoric times: the Aligala rock shelter east of the rock indicates occupation around 3000 BCE, during the Mesolithic Period.

Brahmi inscriptions on the western side show that the many rock shelters and caves nearby were occupied by Buddhist monks and ascetics from as early as the 1st or 2nd century BCE. Monastic settlements were established in the 3rd century BCE on the western and northern slopes of the boulder-strewn hills. The shelters were made under large boulders, with carved drip ledges around the cave mouths, and inscriptions beside the ledges record their donation to the Buddhist monastic order as residences. These date between the 3rd century BCE and the 1st century CE.
sections.content:
Sigiriya consists of an ancient citadel and was both a palace and a fortress. The ruins include an upper palace on the flat top of the rock, with cisterns cut into the rock, a mid-level terrace that holds the Lion Gate and the mirror wall with its frescoes, and lower palaces clinging to the slopes below. The moats, walls and gardens extended for a few hundred metres from the base of the rock. On a small plateau about halfway up the rock stood a gateway in the form of an enormous lion, from which the name Sinhagiri, the Lion Rock, derives. A sculpted lion's head once stood above the legs and paws flanking the entrance, but the head collapsed years ago.

The site plan combined symmetry and asymmetry. On the west side of the rock lay a park for the royals laid out on a symmetrical plan, with water-retaining structures and hydraulic systems, some of which work today. The south holds a man-made reservoir. The gardens fall into three linked forms: water gardens, cave and boulder gardens, and terraced gardens. Five gates were placed at the entrances, and the more elabourate western gate is thought to have been reserved for the royals.
sections.making:
The Cūḷavaṃsa, an ancient Sri Lankan chronicle, describes the making of Sigiriya. It records that in 477 CE Kashyapa I, the son of King Dhatusena by a non-royal consort, seized the throne in a coup assisted by Migara, the king's nephew and army commander. Kashyapa murdered his father by walling him up alive and usurped a throne that rightfully belonged to his half-brother Moggallana, who fled to South India and vowed revenge.

Expecting Moggallana's return, Kashyapa moved his capital and residence from Anuradhapura to the more secure summit of Sigiriya. During his reign, 477 to 495 CE, Sigiriya was developed into a complex city and fortress, and most of the elabourate constructions on the summit and around it, including defensive structures, palaces and gardens, date from this period. According to the chronicle, the area had been a large forest that became a hill after storms and landslides. Alternative stories name Dhatusena as the primary builder, with Kashyapa finishing the work in honour of his father, and still other accounts describe Kashyapa as a playboy king whose pleasure palace this was.
sections.reception:
The frescoes were praised by John Still, who wrote in 1907 that "the whole face of the hill appears to have been a gigantic picture gallery" and "the largest picture in the world perhaps". The paintings would have covered most of the western face of the rock, an area 140 metres long and 40 metres high, and graffiti refer to 500 ladies in them. Although classified as belonging to the Anuradhapura period, their style is considered unique, with lines that enhance the sense of volume of the figures. The identity of the ladies has not been confirmed: some believe they were the ladies of the kings, others that they were women taking part in religious observances. The pictures resemble paintings in the Ajanta Caves in India.

Visitors from the 8th century onward scribbled verses on the mirror wall, most of them in the 9th and 10th centuries. People of all walks of life wrote there, from poets to provincial governors to housewives. Of more than 1,500 poems, most are addressed to the ladies of the frescoes: men praised their beauty and women shared their envy. Senarath Paranavithana, the Archaeological Commissioner of Ceylon, deciphered 685 verses.
sections.survival:
When Moggallana arrived he declared war and defeated Kashyapa in 495 CE. The Cūḷavaṃsa and folklore say that Kashyapa's army abandoned him after misreading a change of course by his war elephant as a retreat, and that he took his own life with a blade; in other versions he is assassinated by poison administered by a concubine. Moggallana returned the capital to Anuradhapura and converted Sigiriya into a Buddhist monastery complex, which survived until the 13th or 14th century. No records are found from then until the 16th and 17th centuries, when it was used briefly as an outpost of the Kingdom of Kandy.

In 1831 Major Jonathan Forbes of the 78th (Highlanders) Regiment of Foot, returning on horseback from Pollonnuruwa, encountered the brushwood-covered summit. Antiquarians and later archaeologists took an interest, and work began on a small scale in the 1890s, with H.C.P. Bell the first to research the site extensively. On 14 October 1967 paint was splashed on the frescoes; Luciano Maranzi, trained in Rome, assisted the restoration, which ended on 11 April 1968. A report presented in 2010 suggested that the 22 frescoes have been fading since 1930, and writing on the mirror wall is now banned.
sections.legacy:
Sigiriya is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and is regarded as one of the best preserved examples of ancient urban planning. It is considered one of the most important urban planning sites of the first millennium, with a plan described as very elabourate and imaginative. The Cultural Triangle Project, launched by the Government of Sri Lanka, turned its attention to Sigiriya in 1982, and archaeological work began on the entire city for the first time under it.

Its gardens are counted among the oldest landscaped gardens in the world. Senake Bandaranayake identifies three traditions of landscape gardening there: the symmetrical water gardens, the asymmetrical cave and boulder gardens, and the terraced gardens at the base of the rock; he suggests that the palace garden on the summit combines all three. Interpretations of the site differ. Some regard it as the work of a Buddhist community without a military function, and it may have been important in the competition between the Mahayana and Theravada Buddhist traditions in ancient Sri Lanka. Its fountains of circular limestone plates, fed by underground conduits, still work, especially in the rainy season.

summary: Sigiriya, the Lion Rock, is a granite column in Sri Lanka that King Kashyapa made his fortress capital from 477 CE. After his defeat in 495 it became a Buddhist monastery. Its frescoes, mirror wall poems and gardens survive and are a World Heritage Site.
notes: Start: 477 is the year the Cūḷavaṃsa gives for Kashyapa's coup and the move; circa true because alternative stories name Dhatusena as the builder.
Kashyapa's death is told differently: suicide by sword, cutting his own throat, or poison from a concubine; the text gives the variants.
The intro and Wikipedia's lead say the dates CE 477-495; the history says most constructions date from this reign.
Left out: popular culture, UNESCO's inscription year (not given), the Mapagala fortress, Masada and Sherkala (see also).
